techniques.name: Differential Privacy
techniques.description: Differential privacy puts a mathematical limit on what a published result reveals about any one person. The data holder adds random noise, drawn for example from a Laplace or Gaussian distribution, to each answer before release, such as a count, an average or a table of statistics, so the answer would look almost the same with or without any one person's data. The amount of noise depends on how much one person could change the answer (its sensitivity) and on a privacy budget called epsilon, which sets how far the two cases may differ (the Gaussian mechanism adds a second, small parameter, delta, for the chance of exceeding that limit). A smaller epsilon means more noise, a stronger guarantee and less accurate answers, and each release spends part of the budget. The guarantee covers whether a person's data took part, not conclusions about the wider population that the results legitimately show.

example_use_cases.description: A national statistics office adds calibrated noise to published census tables so that no single household's presence changes the results by more than a set amount. Statisticians use the epsilon setting to decide how much accuracy small areas must give up.

A health authority publishes weekly hospital admission counts by postcode district with Laplace noise added, so a rare diagnosis in a small district cannot be tied to one patient. Its privacy officer sets a yearly budget and decides how many weekly releases it can cover.

An analytics team lets internal analysts query customer purchase data only through an interface that adds noise and tracks each analyst's privacy budget. The data protection lead uses the budget log to decide when an analyst must stop querying.

A model-evaluation team publishes noisy aggregate performance counts for declared groups. It documents the protected unit, sensitivity bound, noise mechanism and cumulative privacy budget so reviewers can interpret the release's guarantee.

limitations.description: Noise lowers accuracy, and for a given epsilon the noise on a count does not shrink as the dataset grows, so small groups, rare categories and fine-grained tables suffer most. A strong guarantee (small epsilon) can make statistics for small subgroups unusable.
Setting the privacy budget (epsilon) requires expertise and careful consideration of the privacy-utility trade-off, with no universal guidelines for appropriate values across different applications.

Each release spends part of a fixed privacy budget, and the epsilons add up across releases. Once the budget is spent, no further analysis of the same data is possible without weakening the guarantee, so releases must be planned in advance.

The guarantee depends on correct sensitivity analysis: if a query's sensitivity is underestimated, or one person can contribute many records, too little noise is added and the stated epsilon no longer holds.

The guarantee concerns whether one person's data took part, not what the results show about the population. Conclusions that hold for everyone still apply to each individual, and protection weakens for groups, such as a family, by a factor equal to the group size.

resources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
resources.abstract: The problem of privacy-preserving data analysis has a long history spanning multiple disciplines. As electronic data about individuals becomes increasingly detailed, and as technology enables ever more powerful collection and curation of these data, the need increases for a robust, meaningful, and mathematically rigorous definition of privacy, together with a computationally rich class of algorithms that satisfy this definition. Differential Privacy is such a definition. After motivating and discussing the meaning of differential privacy, the preponderance of this monograph is devoted to fundamental techniques for achieving differential privacy, and application of these techniques in creative combinations, using the query-release problem as an ongoing example. A key point is that, by rethinking the computational goal, one can often obtain far better results than would be achieved by methodically replacing each step of a non-private computation with a differentially private implementation. Despite some astonishingly powerful computational results, there are still fundamental limitations — not just on what can be achieved with differential privacy but on what can be achieved with any method that protects against a complete breakdown in privacy. Virtually all the algorithms discussed herein maintain differential privacy against adversaries of arbitrary computational power. Certain algorithms are computationally intensive, others are efficient. Computational complexity for the adversary and the algorithm are both discussed. We then turn from fundamentals to applications other than queryrelease, discussing differentially private methods for mechanism design and machine learning. The vast majority of the literature on differentially private algorithms considers a single, static, database that is subject to many analyses. Differential privacy in other models, including distributed databases and computations on data streams is discussed. Finally, we note that this work is meant as a thorough introduction to the problems and techniques of differential privacy, but is not intended to be an exhaustive survey — there is by now a vast amount of work in differential privacy, and we can cover only a small portion of it.

resources.title: Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis
The 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System TopDown Algorithm
resources.abstract: The Census TopDown Algorithm (TDA) is a disclosure avoidance system using differential privacy for privacy-loss accounting.The algorithm ingests the final, edited version of the 2020 Census data and the final tabulation geographic definitions.The algorithm then creates noisy versions of key queries on the data, referred to as measurements, using zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy.Another key aspect of the TDA are invariants, statistics that the Census Bureau has determined, as matter of policy, to exclude from the privacyloss accounting.The TDA postprocesses the measurements together with the invariants to produce a Microdata Detail File (MDF) that contains one record for each person and one record for each housing unit enumerated in the 2020 Census.The MDF is passed to the 2020 Census tabulation system to produce the 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File.This article describes the mathematics and testing of the TDA for this purpose.

resources.title: RAPPOR
resources.abstract: Randomized Aggregatable Privacy-Preserving Ordinal Response, or RAPPOR, is a technology for crowdsourcing statistics from end-user client software, anonymously, with strong privacy guarantees. In short, RAPPORs allow the forest of client data to be studied, without permitting the possibility of looking at individual trees. By applying randomized response in a novel manner, RAPPOR provides the mechanisms for such collection as well as for efficient, high-utility analysis of the collected data. In particular, RAPPOR permits statistics to be collected on the population of client-side strings with strong privacy guarantees for each client, and without linkability of their reports. This paper describes and motivates RAPPOR, details its differential-privacy and utility guarantees, discusses its practical deployment and properties in the face of different attack models, and, finally, gives results of its application to both synthetic and real-world data.

sample_claims.text: The published census tables were produced by a mechanism satisfying epsilon-differential privacy with a stated epsilon, so adding or removing any one household changes the probability of any published output by at most a factor of e to the power epsilon
Weekly admission counts are released with Laplace noise calibrated to a sensitivity of one patient, and the total privacy budget spent across all releases is tracked and capped
The analytics interface refuses further queries from an analyst once their allocated privacy budget is spent, so cumulative disclosure about any one individual stays within the agreed bound
Aggregate spending statistics shared with a research partner carry a documented epsilon, which bounds how much the partner can learn about whether any one customer's data was included
The model performance metrics across demographic groups are accompanied by documented privacy budget allocation and noise parameters

techniques.name: Homomorphic Encryption
techniques.description: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data that stays encrypted, so the server never sees the underlying values. The data owner encrypts the inputs, the server performs the arithmetic directly on the encrypted data, and only the holder of the secret key can decrypt the result. For machine learning, the model is first rewritten using operations the scheme supports, such as additions, multiplications and polynomial approximations of other functions. Exact schemes return the same answer as the unencrypted computation, while approximate schemes, often used for neural networks, return a close one. The guarantee is confidentiality of the data while it is processed, on the usual assumption that the server follows the protocol.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group wants a cloud service to score patients' readmission risk without the provider seeing patient records. The hospital encrypts the patient features, the cloud evaluates a logistic regression model on the encrypted values, and the hospital decrypts the scores. A linear model is chosen on purpose, since encrypted computation becomes costly as models get larger.

A bank outsources credit scoring to a third-party cloud host. It encrypts customer financial data under a key that never leaves the bank, so an attacker who breaches the host, or an administrator there, can only copy ciphertexts. The bank checks that the host holds no decryption key and that the chosen parameters meet its required security level.

A research team outsources a genome-wide association study to a cloud server. The team encrypts participants' genotype and phenotype data, the server computes the association statistics on the ciphertexts, and only the final statistics are decrypted. One published prototype handled 1,000 individuals and 131,071 genetic variants in about ten minutes on a 28-core server.

limitations.description: Computation is typically orders of magnitude slower than on unencrypted data and ciphertexts are much larger, so real-time use, large models and large datasets are often out of reach. A published encrypted logistic regression training run took about 116 minutes on a real-world dataset.

Only some computations are practical. Circuit depth is limited by noise growth unless costly bootstrapping resets it, and comparisons and non-polynomial functions, such as most neural-network activations, must be approximated or quantised to integers, which can lower accuracy compared with the unencrypted model.

The usual security model is an honest-but-curious server. Ciphertexts can be altered, so encryption alone gives no assurance that the server ran the intended computation correctly, and a malicious host could return a wrong result that still decrypts without error.

Encryption protects data during processing, not what the result reveals. Whoever decrypts the output can still learn about the model or the data behind it through attacks such as membership inference, and with the approximate CKKS scheme, sharing decrypted results can enable a key-recovery attack.

Correct use needs cryptographic expertise. Choosing scheme parameters, encodings and noise budgets wrongly can leave the system insecure or stop results decrypting correctly, and the right choices differ by scheme and library.

resources.title: Fully homomorphic encryption using ideal lattices
resources.abstract: We propose a fully homomorphic encryption scheme -- i.e., a scheme that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt. Our solution comes in three steps. First, we provide a general result -- that, to construct an encryption scheme that permits evaluation of arbitrary circuits, it suffices to construct an encryption scheme that can evaluate (slightly augmented versions of) its own decryption circuit; we call a scheme that can evaluate its (augmented) decryption circuit bootstrappable.

resources.title: Secure Logistic Regression Based on Homomorphic Encryption: Design and Evaluation
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Learning a model without accessing raw data has been an intriguing idea to security and machine learning researchers for years. In an ideal setting, we want to encrypt sensitive data to store them on a commercial cloud and run certain analyses without ever decrypting the data to preserve privacy. Homomorphic encryption technique is a promising candidate for secure data outsourcing, but it is a very challenging task to support real-world machine learning tasks. Existing frameworks can only handle simplified cases with low-degree polynomials such as linear means classifier and linear discriminative analysis. OBJECTIVE: The goal of this study is to provide a practical support to the mainstream learning models (eg, logistic regression). METHODS: We adapted a novel homomorphic encryption scheme optimized for real numbers computation. We devised (1) the least squares approximation of the logistic function for accuracy and efficiency (ie, reduce computation cost) and (2) new packing and parallelization techniques. RESULTS: Using real-world datasets, we evaluated the performance of our model and demonstrated its feasibility in speed and memory consumption. For example, it took approximately 116 minutes to obtain the training model from the homomorphically encrypted Edinburgh dataset. In addition, it gives fairly accurate predictions on the testing dataset. CONCLUSIONS: We present the first homomorphically encrypted logistic regression outsourcing model based on the critical observation that the precision loss of classification models is sufficiently small so that the decision plan stays still.

resources.title: Optimized homomorphic encryption solution for secure genome-wide association studies
resources.abstract: Background Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) refer to observational studies of a genome-wide set of genetic variants across many individuals to see if any genetic variants are associated with a certain trait. A typical GWAS analysis of a disease phenotype involves iterative logistic regression of a case/control phenotype on a single-neuclotide polymorphism (SNP) with quantitative covariates. GWAS have been a highly successful approach for identifying genetic-variant associations with many poorly-understood diseases. However, a major limitation of GWAS is the dependence on individual-level genotype/phenotype data and the corresponding privacy concerns. Methods We present a solution for secure GWAS using homomorphic encryption (HE) that keeps all individual data encrypted throughout the association study. Our solution is based on an optimized semi-parallel GWAS compute model, a new Residue-Number-System (RNS) variant of the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) HE scheme, novel techniques to switch between data encodings, and more than a dozen crypto-engineering optimizations. Results Our prototype can perform the full GWAS computation for 1,000 individuals, 131,071 SNPs, and 3 covariates in about 10 minutes on a modern server computing node (with 28 cores). Our solution for a smaller dataset was awarded co-first place in iDASH’18 Track 2: “Secure Parallel Genome Wide Association Studies using HE”. Conclusions Many of the HE optimizations presented in our paper are general-purpose, and can be used in solving challenging problems with large datasets in other application domains.

sample_claims.text: The cloud provider processes the hospital's patient records only in encrypted form and holds no key that can decrypt them
Individual-level genotype data stay encrypted at every stage on the analysis server, and only the aggregate association statistics are ever decrypted
A breach of the third-party hosting environment exposes only ciphertexts of the bank's customer data, because the secret key never leaves the bank
Encrypted queries sent to the hosted model reveal neither the client's inputs nor the predictions to the operator, even to an administrator with full access to the server's memory and storage

techniques.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
techniques.description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.

resources.title: Private Ad Modeling with DP-SGD
resources.abstract: A well-known algorithm in privacy-preserving ML is differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). While this algorithm has been evaluated on text and image data, it has not been previously applied to ads data, which are notorious for their high class imbalance and sparse gradient updates. In this work we apply DP-SGD to several ad modeling tasks including predicting click-through rates, conversion rates, and number of conversion events, and evaluate their privacy-utility trade-off on real-world datasets. Our work is the first to empirically demonstrate that DP-SGD can provide both privacy and utility for ad modeling tasks.

sample_claims.text: The credit-default model shared with the partner lender was trained with DP-SGD to epsilon 2 and delta 10^-7, with each customer contributing one training example and the budget computed over every training step by the accountant in Opacus.

The published chest X-ray model weights satisfy differential privacy with epsilon 8 and delta 10^-5 with respect to any one patient, and the hyperparameter search run on patient images is included in that budget.
Training batches were drawn by Poisson sampling, matching the assumption of the privacy accountant that produced the reported epsilon.
The skills-tagging model's privacy budget of epsilon 4 per applicant covers the full fine-tuning run and every hyperparameter trial run on applicants' CVs.
